q: Can I use my GHG Protocol carbon footprint for CBAM, or is CBAM embedded emissions data different?
title: GHG inventory or CBAM embedded emissions?
short: Not directly. A GHG Protocol footprint totals a company's emissions for a year. CBAM needs emissions per tonne of a specific product, calculated for one installation under the EU monitoring rules, including precursors and, for steel and aluminium, direct emissions only. The same invoices feed both, but the boundary and the arithmetic differ.
audience: Indian exporters of steel or aluminium, EU importers

ul: Boundary: the corporate inventory covers the whole company, offices and vehicles included. CBAM covers one installation and its production processes.
Unit: the inventory gives tonnes a year. CBAM gives tonnes CO2e per tonne of goods, by CN code.
Precursors: CBAM adds the embedded emissions of precursors you bought, such as pig iron or unwrought aluminium. In a corporate inventory those sit in Scope 3.
Indirect emissions: the inventory always reports Scope 2. In the CBAM definitive period, electricity emissions count for cement and fertilisers but not for iron and steel, aluminium or hydrogen.
Period and verification: CBAM uses the calendar year, and actual values must be verified by an accredited verifier.

p: Fuel quantities, process inputs such as limestone or electrodes, and electricity units are the same data in both. If your inventory is built from invoices and meter readings by site and month, most of the CBAM activity data is already there. What you add is the split by production process and the production tonnage.

ul: Company-wide totals that mix several sites.
Spend-based estimates; CBAM needs physical quantities.
Factors chosen for the inventory if the CBAM monitoring rules require a different calculation, for example measured carbon content for some process inputs.

p: A buyer or verifier may put your BRSR or CDP footprint next to your CBAM declaration. Reconcile them once a year: installation direct emissions plus other sites and vehicles should come back to your Scope 1. A gap you can explain is fine; a gap you cannot explain invites questions.

example.title: Worked example: a steel rolling unit
lines: Corporate Scope 1: 8,500 t CO2, of which 500 t is trucks and the head office
Installation direct emissions: 8,500 minus 500 = 8,000 t CO2
Production: 20,000 t of covered goods, no precursors bought in
CBAM direct embedded emissions: 8,000 divided by 20,000 = 0.40 t CO2 per t
Scope 2 of 4,000 t stays in the inventory but is not counted in the CBAM figure for steel
example.note: A real unit that buys billets would add their embedded emissions per tonne used; that is often the larger figure.
